¶
'''bee-flower''' (bē′flou″ėr), ''n.'' Same as ''bee-orchis.''

'''bee-fly''' (bē′flī), ''n.'' A dipterous insect, ''Phora incrassata'', which is a formidable pest of the beehive, formerly considered capable of producing the disease called foul-brood. See ''Phoridæ.''

'''beef-measle''' (bēf′mē″zl), ''n.'' The measle of beef; the hydatid or scoleciform stage of the unarmed tapeworm of the ox, ''Tænia mediocanellata.''

'''beefsteak''' (bēf′stāk′), ''n.'' [< ''beef'' + ''steak.'' Adopted in other languages, D. ''biefstuk'' (assimilated to ''stuk'', piece), G. ''beefsteak'', Dan. ''böfsteg'', Sw. ''biffstek'', F. ''bifteck'', Sp. (Cuban) ''bifteq'', It. ''biftecco'', Russ. ''bifsteksŭ'', etc.] A steak or slice of beef, cut from the hind quarter, suitable for broiling or frying.

'''beefsteak-fungus''' (bēf′stāk′fung″gus), ''n.'' An edible hymenomycetous fungus, ''Fistulina hepatica'', belonging to the family ''Polyporei.'' {{smaller|It sometimes attains a large size, and is thought to resemble beefsteak somewhat in appearance.}}

'''beefsteak-plant''' (bēf′stāk′plant), ''n.'' '''1.''' A species of ''Saxifraga'', ''S. sarmentosa'', with fleshy purplish leaves.—'''2.''' A name applied to species of ''Begonia''.

'''beefsuet-tree''' (bēf′sū′et-trē), ''n.'' The buffalo-berry, ''Shepherdia argentea.''

'''beef-tea''' (bēf′tē′), ''n.'' An aqueous extract of beef obtained by soaking and heating chopped beef in water, straining it, and seasoning to taste. {{smaller|It contains salts and extractives, a little gelatin, and fat. It is useful as a stimulant, and forms an appropriate introduction to a meal.}}

'''beef-witted''' (bēf′wit″ed), ''a.'' Having the wit of an ox; dull in intellect; heavy-headed; stupid.

<noinclude><pagequality level="1" user="transcriber" />{{RunningHeader|beech|502|beehive}}</noinclude>{{smaller|places where it is constantly wet. It is manufactured into a great variety of tools, for which it is fitted on account of its great hardness, toughness, and close, uniform texture, and is also used to some extent in making furniture, taking a beautiful polish and varying much in color. Several ornamental varieties are frequently seen, as the red beech and copper beech with colored leaves, and the fern-leafed beech with divided leaves. The American beech, ''F. ferruginea'', is a very similar tree, sometimes 100 feet in height and 3 or 4 feet in diameter.—'''Australian beech,''' ''Tectona australis'', a species of teak.—'''Beech-cherry.''' See ''cherry''.—'''Blue beech.''' Same as ''water-beech''.—'''Seaside beech,''' of the West Indies, ''Exostemma Caribbæum'', a tree belonging to the natural order ''Rubiaceæ''. It is allied to cinchona, and its bark is used as a febrifuge.}}

'''beech<sup>2</sup>†''', ''n.'' Obsolete spelling of ''beach''.

'''beech-coal''' (bēch′kōl), ''n.'' Charcoal from beech-wood.

'''beech-drops''' (bēch′drops), ''n.'' A low annual plant, ''Epiphegus Virginiana'', without green foliage, parasitic upon the roots of the beech in the United States. {{smaller|It belongs to the natural order ''Orobanchaceæ''. ''Albany beech-drops'', or pine-drops, ''Pterospora andromedea'', and ''false beech-drops'', or pine-sap, ''Monotropa Hypopitys'', are similar parasitic plants of the natural order ''Ericaceæ''.}}

'''beechen''' (bē′chen), ''a.''   [< ME. ''bechen'', < AS. ''becen'' (= D. ''beuken'' = OHG. ''buochīn'', MHG. G. ''buchen'' = L. ''fāginus'' = Gr. φήγινος), < ''bōc'', beech, + ''-en'': see ''beech''<sup>1</sup> and ''-en''.]   '''1.''' Of, pertaining to, or derived from the beech: as, ''beechen'' boughs; ''beechen'' shade.
{{smaller block|<poem>His aged head, crowned with ''beechen'' wreath,
Seemed like a poll of ivy in the teeth
Of winter hoar.</poem>
{{right|''Keats.''}}}}
'''2.''' Made of the wood of the beech: as, ''beechen'' vessels.
{{smaller block|<poem>A ''beechen'' bowl,</poem>}}
<poem>A maple dish, my furniture should be;
Crisp, yellow leaves my bed.</poem>
{{smaller block|{{right|''Wordsworth'', Eccles. Sonnets, i. 22.}}}}

'''beech-fern''' (bēch′fėrn), ''n.'' A fern belonging to the genus ''Phegopteris'' (which see).

'''beech-finch''' (bēch′finch), ''n.'' The chaffinch, ''Fringilla cœlebs.''   ''Macgillivray.''

'''beech-fungus''' (bēch′fung″gus), ''n.'' An edible fungus, ''Cyttaria Darwinii'', allied to the morel. {{smaller|It is abundant in Terra del Fuego upon the branches of evergreen beeches, and is at times the principal food of the natives.}}

'''beech-gall''' (bēch′gâl), ''n.'' A gall or excrescence formed on the beech by insects.

'''beech-hopper''' (bēch′hop″ėr), ''n.'' A coleopterous insect, ''Orchestes fagi'', family ''Curculionidæ'', or weevils, injurious to beech-trees, between the two surfaces of the leaves of which they lay their eggs.

'''beech-marten''' (bēch′mär″ten), ''n.'' ''Mustela foina'', one of two species or varieties of the European marten, usually distinguished from the common pine-marten, ''M. martes'', by the white throat and some other external features, as well as by some differences in habits. Also called ''stone-marten.''

'''beech-mast''' (bēch′mȧst), ''n.''   [< ''beech''<sup>1</sup> + ''mast''<sup>2</sup>; = ''buck-mast.'']   The mast or nuts of the beech-tree, from which an oil is obtained. {{smaller|The cake which remains after the oil has been expressed is a good fattening food for oxen, swine, and poultry, but is injurious to horses. See ''beech-oil.''}}

'''beechnut''' (bēch′nut), ''n.'' One of the nuts or fruits of the beech. The nuts are triangular, and inclosed in a spiny capsule or husk.

'''beech-oil''' (bēch′oil), ''n.'' A bland fixed oil expressed from the mast or nuts of the beech-tree. {{smaller|It is used in Picardy and in other parts of France instead of butter; but it is said to occasion heaviness and pains in the stomach.}}

'''beech-owl''' (bēch′owl), ''n.'' A name of the tawny owl or wood-owl of Europe, ''Syrnium aluco.''

'''beech-wheat†'''
(bēch′hwēt), ''n.'' Same as ''buckwheat.''

[[File:century v01 p0528 c1f1.png|center|219px]]
{{c|{{smaller|European Bee-eater (''Merops apiaster'').}}}}

'''beechy''' (bē′chi), ''a.''   [< ''beech''<sup>1</sup> + ''-y''<sup>1</sup>.]   Of, pertaining to, or abounding in beeches: as, “a ''beechy'' garland,” ''Fletcher'', Purple Island, vi.

'''bee-culture''' (bē′kul″tṳ̄r), ''n.'' The rearing of bees in a state of domestication; apiculture.

'''bee-eater''' (bē′ē″tėr), ''n.'' That which eats bees, as a bird; an apiaster. {{smaller|Specifically—(''a'') The European ''Merops apiaster.'' (''b'') ''pl.'' The birds of the family ''Meropidæ'', of which there are several genera and numerous species, chiefly African. See ''Merops'', ''Meropidæ''.}}

'''beef''' (bēf), ''n.''   [Early mod. E. also ''beefe'', ''beafe'', ''biefe'', etc., < ME. ''beef'', ''befe'', ''beof'', ''bouf'', ''boef'', < OF. ''boef'', ''buef'', ''boeuf'' = Pr. ''bov'' = Sp. ''buey'' = Pg. ''boi'' = It. ''bove'' (cf. Sw. ''biff'', Dan. ''böf'', beef, from E.; and see ''beefsteak''), < L. ''bovem'', acc. of ''bos'' (see ''Bos'' and ''bovine''), = Gr. βοῦς, an ox, = Ir. and Gael. ''bo'', a cow, = W. ''buw'' = Skt. ''go'', a cow, = AS. ''cū'', E. ''cow''<sup>1</sup>: see ''cow''<sup>1</sup>, which is thus ult. identical with ''beef''.]   '''1.''' An animal of the bovine genus, whether ox, bull, or cow, in the full-grown state. {{smaller|[In this, which is the original sense, the word has a plural, ''beeves'', formerly sometimes ''beefs''. The singular is nearly obsolete.]}}
{{smaller block|These are the beasts which ye shall eat: the ''beef'', the sheep, and the goat.
{{right|Deut. xiv. 4 (ed. 1578).}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>A pound of man’s flesh, taken from a man,
Is not so estimable, profitable neither,
As flesh of muttons, ''beefs'', or goats.</poem>
{{right|''Shak.'', M. of V., i. 3.}}}}
{{smaller block|A herd of ''beeves'', fair oxen, and fair kine.
{{right|''Milton'', P. L., xi. 647.}}}}
'''2.''' The flesh of an ox, bull, or cow when killed. [In this sense the word has no plural.]—'''3.''' A name given by quarrymen to certain beds of fibrous carbonate of lime occurring in England in the middle division of the Purbeck series, the highest part of the Jurassic.—'''4.''' Brawn; muscularity; weight and strength combined: as, the crew is lacking in ''beef''. [Colloq.]—'''Alamode beef.''' {{smaller|See ''alamode''.}}—'''Baron of beef.''' {{smaller|See ''baron''.}}—'''Collared beef''', {{smaller|beef rolled, boned, slightly salted or corned, and seasoned with herbs and spices.}}—'''Hung beef''', {{smaller|beef cured by being hung up to dry; dried beef.}}—'''Jerked''' beef. {{smaller|See ''jerk''.}}

'''beef-brained†''' (bēf′brānd), ''a.'' Having the brain or wit of an ox; beef-witted: as, “the most ''beef-brained'' sensualist,” ''Turniers'', Cure of Misprision, p. 29 (Ord MS.).

'''beef-cattle''' (bēf′kat″l), ''n. pl.'' Bovine animals adapted or intended for conversion into beef; bovine animals for slaughter.

'''beef-eater''' (bēf′ē″tėr), ''n.''   [< ''beef'' + ''eater''. In sense 2, merely a particular use of the same word; cf. AS. ''hlāf-ǣta'', a domestic servant, lit. ‘loaf-eater,’ contrasting with ''hlāford'', master, lit. ‘loaf-keeper.’ Servants are often thought of as eaters; Ben Jonson uses ''eaters'' in the sense of ‘servants’ (“Epicœne,” iii. 2). The oft-quoted etymology from a supposed *''buffetier'', < ''buffet'', a sideboard, is mere fiction.]   '''1.''' One who eats beef; hence, a well-fed fellow; a stout fleshy man.—'''2.''' One of the yeomen of the English royal guard, who, since the accession of Henry VII. in 1485, have attended the sovereign at state banquets and on other ceremonial occasions. The name is also given to the warders of the Tower of London, who wear a similar uniform. [In this sense commonly without a hyphen.]
{{smaller block|Charles had begun to form a small standing army. He felt that without some better protection than that of the train-bands and ''beef-eaters'' his palace and person would scarcely be secure in the vicinity of a great city swarming with warlike Fifth Monarchy men who had been just disbanded.
{{right|''Macaulay'', Hist. Eng., iii.}}}}
'''3.''' An African insessorial bird, of the genus ''Buphaga'', which feeds on the larvæ that infest the hides of oxen. {{smaller|It is a mere book-name, translating ''Buphaga''; the more frequent term is ''oxpecker''. See ''Buphaga''.}}
'''4.''' Same as ''bluebottle'', 2.

'''beef-witted''' (bēf′wit″ed), ''a.'' Having the wit of an ox; dull in intellect; heavy-headed; stupid. {{smaller block|Thou mongrel, ''beef-witted'' lord! {{right|''Shak.'', T. and C., ii. 1.}}}}

'''beefwood''' (bēf′wu̇d), ''n.''   [< ''beef'' (in allusion to its grain and color) + ''wood.'']   '''1.''' The timber of some species of Australian trees belonging to the genus ''Casuarina'' (which see). {{smaller|It is of a reddish color, hard and close-grained, with dark and whitish streaks. It is used chiefly for fine ornamental work.}}

'''2.''' In the West Indies, a name given to ''Pisonia obtusata'', with soft coarse-grained wood.—{{smaller|'''Red beefwood,''' of Jamaica, ''Ardisia coriacea'', a myrsinaceous shrub.—'''White beefwood,''' ''Schœpfia chrysophylloides'', natural order ''Olacinaceæ''.}}

'''beefy''' (bē′fi), ''a.''   [< ''beef'' + ''-y''<sup>1</sup>.]   '''1.''' Ox-like; hence, fleshy; obese; solid.

{{smaller block|He [Carlyle] was at dinner when a ''beefy'' Tory was declaiming to this effect. {{right|''The American'', VIII. 390.}}}}

'''2.''' Brawny; muscular; hardy. [Colloq.]

'''bee-garden''' (bē′gär″dn), ''n.'' A garden or inclosure to set beehives in; an apiary.   ''Mortimer.''

'''beegerite''' (bē′gėr-īt), ''n.''   [After H. ''Beeger'' of Denver, Colorado.]   A sulphid of bismuth and lead occurring in dark-gray masses with brilliant metallic luster, rarely crystallized, found in Colorado.

'''bee-glue''' (bē′glö), ''n.'' A resinous substance with which bees cement the combs to the hives and close up the cells. Also called ''propolis.''

'''bee-gum''' (bē′gum), ''n.'' In the southern United States, a hollowed section of a gum-tree used as a beehive.

'''bee-hawk''' (bē′hâk), ''n.'' A name of the honey-buzzard of Europe, ''Pernis apivorus'': so called because it preys upon bees, wasps, and other insects.—{{smaller|'''Bee-hawk moth,''' a name of various lepidopterous insects of the families ''Sphingidæ'' and ''Sesiidæ'', and especially of the genera ''Macroglossa'' and ''Sesia''.}}

'''beehead†''' (bē′hed), ''n.'' A crazy or flighty person.

'''beeheaded''' (bē′hed″ed), ''a.''   [=Sc. ''bee-headit.'']   Crazy; flighty.

'''bee-herd''' (bē′hėrd), ''n.'' A person who takes care of bees; a bee-keeper.   ''Phin'', Dict. Apiculture, p. 13.

'''beehive''' (bē′hīv), ''n.''   [< ME. ''beehyve''; < ''bee''<sup>1</sup> + ''hive.'']   '''1.''' A case or box serving as a habitation for bees. See ''hive.''—'''2.''' The common name of a species of medic, ''Medicago scutellata'', from the shape of its spirally coiled pod.—{{smaller|'''Beehive house,''' the popular name of a class of very ancient coni-}}
